🔑 If You Only Remember These

  1. Only the asexual erythrocytic stage of malaria causes clinical symptoms (fever from hemolysis) — liver stage is silent.
  2. Primaquine is the ONLY drug for the liver (radical cure) — it clears hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale. It also is the main gametocidal drug for all 4 species. Requires G6PD testing first and is never given in pregnancy.
  3. Chloroquine is a blood schizonticide only — NOT active against liver hypnozoites or gametocytes. Resistance = PfCRT pumping the drug out of the food vacuole.
  4. Artemisinins are the GOLD STANDARD for malaria — act as free radicals (via Fe activation) that alkylate parasite proteins. Always given in combination therapy (ACT), never alone (short half-life, resistance risk).
  5. Quinine/Quinidine and Artemisinins are first-line for SEVERE (complicated) malaria — both given parenterally (IV).
  6. Mefloquine = "Mind Floats" — hallmark neuropsychiatric toxicity (vivid dreams, psychosis, seizures) plus QT prolongation.
  7. Do NOT combine Mefloquine with Quinine/Quinidine/Halofantrine — additive cardiotoxicity (QT prolongation → arrhythmia).
  8. Pregnancy antifolate/teratogen mnemonic — "Pregnancy Hates Ludicrous PriMaDonA": Halofantrine, Lumefantrine, Primaquine, Malarone, Doxycycline, Antifolates are avoided in pregnancy.
  9. Chloroquine is the preferred/safest antimalarial in pregnancy for chloroquine-sensitive malaria (Category A).
  10. Doxycycline works at the ribosomal 30S, Clindamycin at the 50S — both target the parasite's apicoplast (prokaryote-like organelle) causing "delayed death."
  11. Only 2 drugs act on the electron transport / ubiquinone pathway: Primaquine and Atovaquone.
  12. Antifolates act on parasite-specific DHPS and DHFR — e.g., Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (Fansidar) and Proguanil-Atovaquone (Malarone).
  13. Metronidazole is the DOC for extraluminal/invasive amoebiasis (and for Trichomonas and Giardia) but must be paired with a luminal amoebicide to clear intestinal cysts.
  14. Luminal amoebicides (Diloxanide furoate, Iodoquinol, Paromomycin) treat only the asymptomatic/carrier (cyst) stage — they do NOT reach tissues.
  15. Pentamidine = DOC for early-stage West African sleeping sickness (T. gambiense); Suramin = DOC for early East African (T. rhodesiense); Melarsoprol = DOC for advanced CNS-stage disease (both regions).
  16. Benznidazole and Nifurtimox are both DOC for Chagas disease (T. cruzi) — American trypanosomiasis.
  17. Nematode drugs act mainly by causing paralysis of worms — but mechanism differs: Pyrantel = spastic (depolarizing, persistent ACh release) vs Piperazine = flaccid (blocks ACh response).
  18. Ivermectin does NOT kill adult filarial worms — it only immobilizes/destroys microfilariae, reducing transmission for ~6 months.
  19. Praziquantel is DOC for most cestode/trematode infections (increases Ca²⁺ permeability → paralysis) — including all schistosome species and neurocysticercosis.
  20. Sulfonamide-based drugs (Sulfamethoxazole, Sulfadiazine) inhibit DHPS; Trimethoprim/Pyrimethamine inhibit DHFR — combined they become synergistic and bactericidal, and are given with folinic acid to prevent host toxicity.

I. Introduction to Malaria

The Philippines is highly endemic for malaria. Treatment planning follows the 3 P's: Plasmodium species, Patient status (uncomplicated/complicated), Pharmacology (susceptibility, availability, resistance). Page 1

A. Life Cycle of the Malaria Parasite

MUST KNOW MECHANISM
Page 1 ▾
Core idea: The malaria life cycle involves a parasite (Plasmodium), a mosquito vector (female Anopheles), and a human host. Antimalarials are targeted at specific points in this cycle.
01 | ENTRY OF ETIOLOGIC AGENTInfected female Anopheles mosquito bites → inoculates sporozoites into skin capillaries
↓
02 | DORMANT HEPATIC STAGESporozoites invade liver parenchymal cells → form tissue schizonts (symptom-free) → multiple fission → release numerous merozoites
↓
03 | ASEXUAL ERYTHROCYTIC STAGEMerozoites invade RBCs → multiply asexually → form blood schizonts
↓
04 | SEXUAL STAGESome merozoites mature into male/female gametocytes → ingested by another feeding mosquito → cycle repeats
  • P. falciparum: liver-stage release of merozoites takes 1–12 weeks after the infective bite; only one cycle of hepatic invasion (same for P. malariae) — no true relapse.
  • P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant hepatic hypnozoites that release merozoites over months to years → this is the basis of malaria relapse.
Exam trap: Only the asexual erythrocytic stage causes clinical malaria (high-grade fever from intravascular hemolysis as new merozoites are released). The liver stage is completely symptom-free — a question describing "silent incubation" is pointing to the hepatic stage, not the blood stage.
Mark as reviewed

B. Use of Drugs — Sites of Chemoprophylactic Action

MUST KNOW
Page 1–2▾
  • Causal prophylaxis: started before/upon entry into an endemic area — targets the pre-erythrocytic (liver) stage before it produces the RBC-invading form.
  • Liver form (exoerythrocytic stage) = radical cure — dormant parasites may stay for months/years → main reason for relapse.
  • RBC / erythrocytic (asexual) stage — where clinical symptoms begin; most drugs work here. Plasmodia entering RBCs either (a) destroy the RBC completely and invade another, or (b) transform quietly into gametocytes, perpetuating the cycle via mosquito uptake.
Mark as reviewed

E. Drug Resistance

SHOULD KNOW
Page 2▾
  • Chloroquine was long the drug of choice for P. falciparum — now resistant in most areas of the world.
  • Resistant strains increase with increasing frequency of drug use (e.g., sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia).
  • Resistance to chloroquine, sulfadoxine, pyrimethamine, mefloquine, and halofantrine has emerged in South America, Brazil, Myanmar, and India.
  • Associated with an overall doubling of childhood mortality from malaria, with increases as high as 11-fold in certain areas.
Mark as reviewed
RECALL CHECK — Section I (5 questions)

1. Which stage of the malaria life cycle actually causes clinical symptoms?
Answer: The asexual erythrocytic stage (via hemolysis when new merozoites are released).

2. Which two Plasmodium species form hypnozoites, and why does this matter clinically?
Answer: P. vivax and P. ovale — hypnozoites cause relapse months to years later; only Primaquine clears them (radical cure).

3. Fill in the blank: Causal prophylaxis targets the ______ stage, before the parasite reaches the blood.
Answer: pre-erythrocytic (liver) stage.

4. Which molecular transporter is the number one reason Plasmodium becomes chloroquine-resistant?
Answer: PfCRT (P. falciparum chloroquine resistance transporter) — pumps the drug out of the food vacuole.

5. Name the only drug that provides radical (liver) cure.
Answer: Primaquine.

II. Tactics — Patient Status & Drug Targets

A. Patient Status — Uncomplicated vs Complicated

MUST KNOW
Page 3▾
Uncomplicated (simple)Complicated (severe)
Fever, chills, diaphoresis, headaches, nausea/vomiting, body aches, general malaise.
→ Treat with oral antimalarials.
Blood is best drawn during high fever/chills — when merozoites are expunging from RBCs. 		Impaired consciousness/coma, severe normocytic anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema, ARDS, circulatory shock, DIC, spontaneous bleeding, acidosis, hemoglobinuria, convulsions, parasitemia >5%. Shock = worst complication.
→ Requires aggressive parenteral treatment (100% bioavailability, fastest absorption).
  • Malaria sensitive (uncomplicated) → Chloroquine ± Primaquine.
  • Malaria resistant (still uncomplicated) → Mefloquine ± Primaquine (prophylaxis), Artemether+Lumefantrine (Coartem), Atovaquone+Proguanil (Malarone), Quinine+Doxycycline/Clindamycin, or Artemisinin therapy. GOLD STANDARD = Artemisinin therapy.
  • Complicated, worsening symptoms → give IV; once stable, shift to oral (oral Coartem). Need BOTH parenteral + oral medications during the transition.
FROM LECTURE — MNEMONIC
  • "PriM and PROPer" — Pri = Primaquine, M = Mefloquine, PROP(er) = prophylaxis for resistant/uncomplicated strains.
  • "COMA pxs. needs QiD CAT scan" — memory cue that a comatose (complicated/severe) patient needs urgent workup.
  • "M'Arte Queens in Severe COMA needs Parenteral (IV/IM) & oral medication" — complicated malaria needs both IV/IM AND oral therapy (Mefloquine, Artesunate/Artemether = "M'Arte", Quinine/Quinidine = "Queens").

Exam trap: Atovaquone + Proguanil (Malarone) is on the "avoid" list in some contexts but the lecture also states it can still be given, especially in the 2nd/3rd trimester, with insufficient early-trimester data (not an outright contraindication like Primaquine/Doxycycline).

D. Drug Regimen Variables

SHOULD KNOW
Page 3▾

A drug regimen for malaria depends on:

  • Clinical status of the patient
  • Type/species of the infecting parasite
  • Area where infection was acquired and its drug-resistance status
  • Whether the patient is pregnant
  • History of drug allergies or other medications taken

Clinically, antimalarials are classified as agents for:

  • Prophylaxis — preventing malaria in people residing in/traveling through an endemic zone
  • Treating acute blood-stage malaria
  • Eliminating hypnozoite liver-stage infections

F. Heme Metabolism Pathway

MUST KNOW MECHANISM
Page 4▾
  • Parasites have limited de novo amino acid synthesis and rely on amino acids released from ingested host hemoglobin.
  • Plasmodial proteases (plasmepsins, falcipain, falcilysin) degrade hemoglobin into amino acids + a toxic metabolite: ferriprotoporphyrin IX (heme).
  • This toxic metabolite is normally detoxified by polymerization into harmless hemozoin.
Hemoglobindegraded by plasmodial proteases (plasmepsins, falcipain, falcilysin)
↓
Amino acids + Ferriprotoporphyrin IX (toxic heme)
↓ (normally)
Hemozoin (polymerized heme, non-toxic)
  • Chloroquine, Halofantrine, and other quinine-type antimalarials inhibit detoxification of ferriprotoporphyrin IX → causes lysosomal membrane damage and toxicity to the parasite. Chloroquine promotes destruction/breaking of heme through alkylation.
  • Resistance: PfCRT (a mutated transmembrane protein) pumps protonated chloroquine out of the food vacuole — the number one reason drugs become resistant ("they kick the drug out from the inside").
  • Artemisinins disrupt heme metabolism differently — through formation of free radicals after activation of free/heme-bound iron, promoting destruction/breaking of proteins. This is why Artemisinins are the GOLD STANDARD — the radical destroys the parasite from within by destroying enzymes/proteins needed for survival.
  • Lumefantrine and Pyronaridine modulate hemoglobin metabolism by forming a complex with hematin, blocking its spontaneous polymerization to beta-hematin/hemozoin — leaving toxic hematin in the food vacuole to enhance hematin-induced RBC lysis.

⚖ Do not confuse: Chloroquine-type MOA vs Artemisinin MOA

Chloroquine / Halofantrine / quinines
Inhibit detoxification of ferriprotoporphyrin IX → toxic heme accumulates → damages the parasite. Mechanism = alkylation of heme.
Artemisinins
Form free radicals after Fe activation → radicals alkylate multiple parasite proteins directly (not just heme) → widespread protein dysfunction → parasite death. This is the GOLD STANDARD mechanism.
Fast distinction: Chloroquine-type drugs block heme detoxification (indirect toxicity via heme buildup); Artemisinins directly generate radicals that alkylate parasite proteins (direct, broad-spectrum protein damage).
Mark as reviewed

G. Electron Transport Pathway

MUST KNOW MECHANISM
Page 4▾

Only 2 drugs act here: Primaquine and Atovaquone — both act on ubiquinone (Q).

Reduced Dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase (DHODH)needs oxidized ubiquinone to regenerate — required for pyrimidine synthesis
↓ ubiquinone (Q) shuttles electrons
Cytochrome bc1 complex → Cytochrome c → Cytochrome c oxidasegenerates H⁺ gradient used to make ATP
  • Atovaquone is a structural analog of ubiquinone — inhibits the interaction between reduced ubiquinone and the Cytochrome BC1 complex, disrupting electron transport and preventing Plasmodia from replicating their DNA (via disrupted pyrimidine synthesis).
  • Primaquine causes nonspecific oxidative damage to plasmodial mitochondria via its metabolite quinone, which substitutes for ubiquinone and inhibits electron transport.
  • A single point mutation in the Cytochrome BC1 complex can render Plasmodia resistant to Atovaquone — this is why Atovaquone is never used alone (always combined, e.g., with Proguanil in Malarone).
Mark as reviewed

H. Protein Translation Pathway

SHOULD KNOW MECHANISM
Page 4–5▾

Doxycycline, Tetracycline, and Clindamycin disrupt malarial protein synthesis by targeting the apicoplast — a semi-autonomous, prokaryote-like organelle in P. falciparum that encodes proteins necessary for survival.

  • Doxycycline works at the 30S ribosomal subunit.
  • Clindamycin acts at the 50S ribosomal subunit.
  • Loss of apicoplast activity manifests as a delayed death response in the parasite.
  • Like bacteria, plasmodial drug resistance here is due to increased activity of transport systems that pump the drug out of the cell.
Mark as reviewed

I. Folate Metabolism Pathway

MUST KNOW MECHANISM
Page 5▾

Folic acid is required for DNA/RNA synthesis. In plasmodial parasites and bacteria, folate is synthesized de novo, making it a useful selective drug target (humans obtain folate from diet, not de novo synthesis in the same pathway).

  • Antifolate drugs act against parasite-specific isoforms of dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) and dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).
  • Combination therapies like sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine act slowly against blood schizonts.
  • Resistance is primarily due to mutations of both DHPS and DHFR — widespread in Southeast Asia, South America, and increasingly Africa.
  • Pyrimethamine acts on the second step of folic acid synthesis (DHFR).
Mark as reviewed
RECALL CHECK — Section II (6 questions)

1. What is the GOLD STANDARD treatment for severe/complicated malaria?
Answer: Artemisinins (IV), often paired with Quinine/Quinidine.

2. Which two drugs must NEVER be given during pregnancy per the "PriMaDonA" mnemonic, besides Primaquine and Malarone/Doxycycline?
Answer: Halofantrine and Lumefantrine (plus antifolates).

3. Name the transporter responsible for chloroquine resistance and what it does.
Answer: PfCRT — pumps protonated chloroquine out of the parasite's food vacuole.

4. Which two drugs act on the electron transport chain via ubiquinone?
Answer: Primaquine and Atovaquone.

5. Doxycycline acts on the ____S ribosomal subunit; Clindamycin acts on the ____S subunit.
Answer: 30S; 50S.

6. What two parasite enzymes do antifolate drugs target?
Answer: Dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) and dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

III. Antimalarial Drugs (Individual Agents)

Drugs used for: Tissue schizonticide + gametocidal (Primaquine) · Tissue schizonticide (Atovaquone, Proguanil) · Blood schizonticide (Chloroquine, Amodiaquine/Piperaquine, Mefloquine, Quinine/Quinidine, Halofantrine/Lumefantrine, Antifolates) · Blood schizonticide + gametocidal (Artemisinins). Page 5

A. Chloroquine

MUST KNOW
Page 5▾
Core idea: Quinolone compound (discovered in plants 2000 years ago). CDC-recommended treatment/chemoprophylaxis for ALL malaria forms from chloroquine-sensitive areas. Highly effective blood schizonticide but NOT active against liver-stage parasites, dormant forms of P. vivax/ovale, or gametocytes.
  • MOA: Prevents detoxification of ferriprotoporphyrin IX; prevents biocrystallization of heme into hemozoin.
  • Resistance: associated with PfCRT (kicks the drug out of the food vacuole — "number one reason" for resistance).
  • PK/PD: half-life ~3–5 days. Drug of choice for chloroquine-sensitive malaria in pregnancy (common prophylactic regimen 500 mg once weekly).
  • Adverse reactions: Parenteral use → severe hypotension, respiratory/cardiac arrest. High doses → irreversible ototoxicity, retinopathy, myopathy, peripheral neuropathy. Rare: hemolysis, confusion, psychosis, seizure, agranulocytosis, exfoliative dermatitis. At therapeutic doses, ADRs are generally uncommon.
  • Contraindications/cautions: commonly causes pruritus in darkly pigmented individuals; can exacerbate psoriasis and porphyria (linked to hemoglobin breakdown). Caution in neurologic/hematologic disorders like G6PD deficiency.
  • NOTE: Relatively SAFE in pregnancy, for young children, and used for MOST blood stages of the parasite.
  • Off-label uses: rheumatoid arthritis, extraintestinal amoebiasis, discoid lupus erythematosus, lepra reaction, infectious mononucleosis, Giardiasis.
Mark as reviewed

B. Amodiaquine & Piperaquine

MUST KNOW
Page 5–6▾
  • Chemically related to Chloroquine → share its MOA. Both effective blood schizonticides (erythrocytic stage).
  • Resistance noted when used as single therapy → WHO recommends combination with Artemisinins: Artesunate+Amodiaquine (Arsucam/ASAQ, first line in Africa) and Dihydroartemisinin+Piperaquine (Artekin, first line in Southeast Asia). First-line for uncomplicated P. falciparum in many countries.
  • Advantage: target chloroquine-resistant strains of P. falciparum; toxicity uncommon.
  • PK: longer half-life than chloroquine → longer post-treatment prophylaxis, good compliance. Amodiaquine ~14 days; Piperaquine ~28 days.
  • Adverse effects: long-term/serious — granulocytosis, aplastic anemia, hepatotoxicity. At standard dosage, non-teratogenic → useful with artemisinins in pregnancy (2nd & 3rd trimester per WHO). Well tolerated short-term (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness); Piperaquine has fewer side effects than Amodiaquine.
Mark as reviewed

C. Quinine & Quinidine

MUST KNOW
Page 6▾
  • Derived from bark of the cinchona tree; traditionally used for intermittent fever.
  • Effective blood schizonticides for all 4 species; parenteral treatment of complicated/severe falciparum malaria. Gametocidal for P. vivax & P. ovale but NOT P. falciparum.
  • FIRST LINE for severe P. falciparum malaria (IV); SAFE in pregnancy (2nd/3rd tri) and children. Intercalates into DNA, disrupting replication/transcription — good for severe disease.
  • Quinine dosing in children: loading dose 20 mg/kg, then 7.5 mg/kg every 8h. Once recovering, oral 8 mg/kg every 8h.
  • Mefloquine (grouped in lecture discussion here) is Category B; CDC recommends monotherapy in the 1st trimester with no increased pregnancy loss/malformation risk; safe for pregnancy and children >5kg, but not infants <1 year.
FROM LECTURE — MNEMONIC
"QUeen B-UCCHHH" — Adverse effects of Quinine/Quinidine:
  • Blackwater fever (rare hypersensitivity → hemolysis)
  • Uterine contractions (mild, esp. 3rd trimester — UNIQUE to quinine/quinidine)
  • Cinchonism (tinnitus, headache, dizziness, blurred vision)
  • Cardiotoxicity (prolonged QT — worse when combined with Primaquine, Halofantrine, Mefloquine)
  • Hematologic toxicity (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis — chloroquine also causes this)
  • Hypoglycemia (increased insulin release)
  • Hypersensitivity (rash, urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm)
  • Contraindications: G6PD deficiency, cardiac abnormalities, renal insufficiency, visual/auditory problems.
  • Drug interactions: NOT with Mefloquine (cardiotoxic) or antacids (↓ absorption). Fast IV infusion → thrombophlebitis, severe hypotension.
  • Regarded as safe at any stage of pregnancy for therapeutic IV use, but conflicting data on oxytocic uterine effects — needs close monitoring.
Mark as reviewed

D. Mefloquine

MUST KNOW
Page 6▾
  • Quinoline compound structurally related to chloroquine.
  • First-line for resistant strains and uncomplicated P. falciparum in combination with IV Artesunate (mostly Asia, South America): uncomplicated→complicated pathway = (1) Artesunate → stabilize → (2) oral Mefloquine.
  • Suppressive blood schizonticide (erythrocytic stage). First-line weekly prophylaxis in ALL geographic areas with chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum.
  • MOA: same as chloroquine (interferes with heme detoxification).
  • PK: half-life ~14–20 days (longest) → once-weekly prophylaxis. Peak plasma at ~18h; given 1–2 weeks before travel; taken once weekly (addresses compliance).
FROM LECTURE — MNEMONIC
"Mefloquine = Mind Floats" — hallmark neuropsychiatric toxicity.
  • ADRs (high doses reach brain & heart): serious neuropsychiatric toxicity — vivid dreams, nightmares, insomnia, depression, seizures, psychosis. Cardiac conduction abnormalities — prolonged QT, arrhythmias.
  • Contraindications: epilepsy, psychiatric disorders, arrhythmias, cardiac conduction defects, CNS/CVS dysfunction.
  • Do NOT co-administer with quinine, quinidine, primaquine, or halofantrine — additive cardiovascular toxicity.
Mark as reviewed

E. Artemisinins

MUST KNOWMECHANISM
Page 6–7▾
Core idea: GOLD STANDARD for treating malaria. Used for both uncomplicated and complicated disease; recommended in pregnancy (2nd/3rd trimester and children); IV artesunate is safe in all trimesters including the 1st when severe malaria makes other options unsuitable.
  • Forms free radical compounds → plasmodial death via alkylation of many proteins (e.g., heme). Rapid decrease in parasitemia and rapid symptom resolution.
  • First-line for uncomplicated AND complicated malaria; also effective against young gametocytes. Blood schizonticide for all malarial species.
  • Combination therapy (ACT) protects against resistance and recrudescence — standard of care in nearly all endemic areas. Rationale: reduces required exposure to each individual drug (limits toxicity) and decreases the chance resistant strains survive/proliferate.

Mechanism of Action — step by step

Hemoglobin digestion releases Fe(II)
↓
Fe(II) attacks artemisinin's peroxide (O–O) bond
↓
Peroxide bond cleaves → unstable oxygen-centered radicals
↓
Radicals rearrange → carbon-centered radicals
↓
Carbon-centered radicals form covalent bonds with parasite proteins (alkylation)
↓
Widespread protein alkylation → loss of parasite viability

PK/PD: Half-life very short — do not use alone for chemoprophylaxis. Artesunate & dihydroartemisinin (water soluble): 30–60 min. Artemether (lipid soluble): 2–3 hours.

ADRs: overall safe (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). Rare: neutropenia, anemia, hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, allergic reactions (~1 in 2,000 patients). Even considered safe for young infants/breastfeeding given the short half-life and general tolerability.

Table 5. Artemisinin-Based Combination Therapies (ACTs)

Artesunate-amodiaquine (ASAQ, Arsucam, Coarsucam)First-line in many African countries
Artesunate-mefloquineFirst-line in Southeast Asia and South America

Exam trap: Artemisinins are always used in combination therapy. WHO has banned standalone artemisinin monotherapy products — the partner drug (e.g., lumefantrine) clears residual parasites and prevents recrudescence/resistance.

G. Pyronaridine

SHOULD KNOW
Page 7–8▾
  • Combined with Artesunate (Pyramax): blood schizonticide against P. falciparum & P. vivax in adults and children.
  • Used for uncomplicated and multi-drug-resistant P. falciparum malaria.
  • MOA: similar to other quinine-type drugs (inhibits hemozoin formation).
  • Most common ADRs resemble malaria symptoms itself; liver enzyme elevation returns to normal after ~1 week.
  • Well tolerated (safe >5 kg) but can cause dizziness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, eosinophilia, transaminitis.
  • Pregnancy: caution (embryotoxic in rodents); has been used successfully mid-to-late trimester in Africa; excreted in breast milk in rat studies — weigh benefits of breastfeeding vs infant exposure risk.
  • Pyramax dosed by body weight; oral suspension established safe/effective for infants/children 5 kg to <20 kg.

H. Electron Transport Inhibitors — Atovaquone, Proguanil, Primaquine

MUST KNOW
Page 8▾

1. Atovaquone

  • MOA: structural analog of ubiquinone; inhibits interaction between reduced ubiquinone and Cytochrome BC1 complex → disrupts electron transport at the cytochrome-b complex. Never used as a single agent (history of resistance).
  • Given as fixed-dose combo with Proguanil (Malarone) — effective against BOTH pre-erythrocytic AND erythrocytic schizonts (once daily). Advantage over mefloquine/doxycycline: shorter prophylaxis period — only ~1 week after exposure.
  • Usual combo: Atovaquone 250 mg + Proguanil 100 mg — highly effective for treatment AND prophylaxis of falciparum malaria. Targets tissue schizonts + erythrocytic schizonts → shorter treatment.
  • Pregnancy/children: well tolerated in non-pregnant; regarded safe in pregnancy but safer in 2nd/3rd trimester; safe for children >5 kg.
  • ADRs: generally well tolerated. High doses: GIT disturbances, ↑ liver enzymes, headache, insomnia, occasional rash.

2. Proguanil (antifolate)

  • Prodrug that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, interfering with folic acid synthesis. Active against both tissue and erythrocytic schizonts.
  • Cautioned in pregnancy — preferably given in 2nd/3rd trimester. Part of the "Hates Ludicrous PriMaDonA" antifolate group.

3. Primaquine

  • IMPORTANT: Drug of Choice for P. vivax & P. ovale — clears dormant liver hypnozoites (pre-erythrocytic & exo-erythrocytic) and has gametocidal effect against ALL 4 malarial species.
  • MOA: metabolites disrupt mitochondrial metabolic processes including electron transport activity. Used predominantly as terminal prophylaxis to clear hepatic hypnozoites.
  • Combined with Chloroquine: Chloroquine eradicates erythrocytic forms; Primaquine targets hepatic forms; Primaquine also renders P. falciparum gametocytes non-infective to mosquitoes.
  • ADRs: generally well tolerated at recommended doses. Higher doses: nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, headache. Rare: leukopenia, agranulocytosis, leukocytosis, cardiac arrhythmias.
  • AVOID in: G6PD deficiency (hemolysis/methemoglobinemia risk), granulocytopenia, methemoglobinemia, patients on myelosuppressive drugs, and pregnancy (fetal RBC hemolysis risk — crosses the placenta). Discontinue if hemolysis or anemia occurs.
  • NEVER administer during pregnancy — crosses placenta, causes in-utero hemolysis of fetal erythrocytes.
  • Other use: treatment adjunct for Pneumocystis jirovecii.
FROM LECTURE — MNEMONIC
"Prime Qu²eens ACTing" — Gametocidal drugs: Primaquine, Quinine/Quinidine, Artemisinins (ACT: Artesunate, Artemether, Dihydroartemisinin).
Mark as reviewed

MUST KNOW

  • Antifolate combinations are highly effective against blood schizont stages of all 4 human malarial species.

  • CQ = Cheap & Quick — Chloroquine for simple malaria (but resistance common)
  • Queen Quinine — severe malaria, but toxic

  • Prima = Primary for P. vivax/P. ovale — prevents relapse

Stages of malaria drugs organize around: Erythrocytic asexual stage (most clinical S/Sx), Dormant hepatic stage (hypnozoites, esp. P. vivax/ovale), Gametocytes (prevents sexual-phase transmission).

RECALL CHECK — Section III (8 questions)

1. What is the "number one reason" drugs like chloroquine become resistant?
Answer: PfCRT pumps the drug out of the food vacuole.

2. Which antimalarial has the longest half-life among the blood schizonticides discussed (~28 days)?
Answer: Piperaquine.

3. Sequence recall — for complicated resistant P. falciparum, what is given first, IV or oral?
Answer: IV (parenteral) first — e.g., IV Artesunate — then switch to oral once stable.

4. Which drug combination is contraindicated due to additive cardiotoxicity: Mefloquine + ______?
Answer: Quinine, Quinidine, Primaquine, or Halofantrine.

5. Cause and effect: Why is Atovaquone never given alone?
Answer: A single point mutation in Cytochrome BC1 can cause resistance — must be combined (e.g., with Proguanil as Malarone).

6. Which drug renders P. falciparum gametocytes non-infective to mosquitoes?
Answer: Primaquine.

7. Doxycycline vs Clindamycin — which is safe in pregnancy and children?
Answer: Clindamycin.

8. What must accompany Fansidar/Proguanil use in pregnancy to protect the fetus?
Answer: High-dose folate supplementation (5 mg daily).

C. Fermentation Pathway (Drug Target)

MUST KNOWMECHANISM
Page 10▾

Amoebae are obligate fermenters of glucose to ethanol for energy. They lack human fermentation enzymes (lactate dehydrogenase, pyruvate decarboxylase, oxidative phosphorylation enzymes). Instead, they use pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) for electron transfer.

Pyruvate
   │  (via PFOR + ferredoxin domain)
   ▼
Acetyl-CoA + reduced ferredoxin
   │
   ├── Reduced ferredoxin → reduces protons → H₂ gas
   ├── Reduced ferredoxin → reduces NADP⁺ → NADPH
   └── Acetyl-CoA → (alcohol dehydrogenase E / AdHE) → Ethanol (energy source)
  • Ferredoxins are iron-sulfur centers that transfer electrons under strongly reducing conditions.
  • Anaerobic bacteria (e.g., H. pylori, Clostridium) express similar PFORs, ferredoxins, and AdHEs.
  • This pathway is a pivotal drug target:
  • Metronidazole — a prodrug activated through interaction with reduced ferredoxin or specific nitroreductases.
  • Nitazoxanide — interferes with PFOR-dependent electron transfer essential for anaerobic energy metabolism.
Mark as reviewed

FROM LECTURE
Metronidazole/Tinidazole is considered the gold standard drug for treating E. histolytica, especially in extraluminal stages.

⚖ Do not confuse: Luminal amoebicides vs Metronidazole/Tinidazole

Luminal amoebicides (Diloxanide, Iodoquinol, Paromomycin)
Act ONLY on cysts within the bowel lumen. Used for asymptomatic/carrier stage. Cannot reach tissue.
Metronidazole/Tinidazole
Reach tissues — used for migrating trophozoites and extraintestinal disease (e.g. liver abscess). Must still be paired with a luminal agent to clear residual cysts.
Fast distinction: Symptomatic or invasive disease always needs Metronidazole/Tinidazole PLUS a luminal amoebicide — never luminal agents alone for active disease.

1. Why are luminal amoebicides insufficient for symptomatic amoebiasis?

FROM LECTURE — MOA MNEMONICS
  • Metronidazole/Tinidazole: "Metro = DNA wreck" — reduced cytotoxic compounds bind DNA → damage
  • Emetine/Dehydroemetine: "Emetine = Empty protein" — inhibits protein synthesis (ribosomal translocation)
  • Nitazoxanide: "Nita knocks PFOR" — blocks pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase
  • Albendazole/Mebendazole: "Bend the Tubules" — bind β-tubulin → inhibit microtubule polymerization
  • Pyrantel pamoate: "Persistent Pyrantel Paralysis" — persistent ACh release → spastic paralysis
  • Piperazine: "Pipe blocks ACh" — blocks ACh response → flaccid paralysis
  • Ivermectin: "Iver = GABA giver" — enhances GABA transmission → paralysis
  • Praziquantel: "Prazi = Calcium Crazy" — ↑ Ca²⁺ permeability → contraction → paralysis
  • Niclosamide: "Nick the ATP" — inhibits oxidative phosphorylation
  • Bithionol: "Bi = Block cAMP" — inhibits adenylyl cyclase → ↓ cAMP

RECALL CHECK — Section VI (6 questions)

1. Which benzimidazole has the highest bioavailability?
Answer: Albendazole.

2. DOC for cutaneous larva migrans?
Answer: Thiabendazole.

3. Compare paralysis type: Pyrantel vs Piperazine.
Answer: Pyrantel = spastic (persistent depolarization); Piperazine = flaccid (blocks ACh response).

4. First-line drug for onchocerciasis today (vs the older 2nd-line agent)?
Answer: Ivermectin is 1st-line; Diethylcarbamazine is 2nd-line.

5. DOC for all schistosome species and neurocysticercosis?
Answer: Praziquantel.

6. What causes the rash sometimes seen with Bithionol or DEC therapy?
Answer: Protein released from dying worms/microfilariae — not direct drug toxicity.

VII. Review Questions (from Lecture) — Answer Key

1. Which of the following antimalarial drugs is used as a gametocidal agent?

  1. Doxycycline
  2. Proguanil
  3. Primaquine
  4. Chloroquine
Show answer
C. Primaquine. Mnemonic: "Prime Qu²eens ACTing" — Primaquine, Quinine/Quinidine, Artemisinins (ACT: Artesunate, Artemether, Dihydroartemisinin).

2. An effective blood schizonticide also used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis:

  1. Doxycycline
  2. Proguanil
  3. Primaquine
  4. Chloroquine
Show answer
D. Chloroquine. Off-label uses: rheumatoid arthritis, extraintestinal amoebiasis, discoid lupus erythematosus, lepra reaction, infectious mononucleosis, Giardiasis.

3. This antimalarial drug can kill the late tissue schizonts of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale:

  1. Doxycycline
  2. Mefloquine
  3. Primaquine
  4. Chloroquine
Show answer
C. Primaquine — used for the dormant (hypnozoite) stages of malaria.

4. A 41-year-old woman is about to take a trip to Kenya and seeks a drug due to malaria prevalence. Her doctor gave a drug taken once a week, good for chloroquine-resistant strains of P. falciparum. Which drug did she receive?

  1. Proguanil-atovaquone
  2. Mefloquine
  3. Quinine
  4. Amodiaquine
Show answer
B. Mefloquine — once-weekly prophylaxis; first-line weekly prophylaxis in all areas with chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum. (Reference table shows the chemoprophylaxis regimens for Atovaquone-proguanil, Mefloquine, Doxycycline, Primaquine, Chloroquine.)

5. A 32-year-old woman complained of sudden increase in heart rate. Four days earlier she was hospitalized for presumptive malaria; P. vivax infection was confirmed and appropriate therapy started. ECG showed torsades de pointes. Which drug most likely caused this arrhythmia?

  1. Quinine
  2. Chloroquine
  3. Malarone
  4. Pyronaridine
Show answer
A. Quinine. CVS toxicity (QT prolongation → torsades) is classically associated with: Quinidine, Mefloquine, Primaquine, Halofantrine — and Quinine shares this cardiotoxic profile (per the "QUeen B-UCCHHH" mnemonic).

Commonly Confused Concepts

⚖ Do not confuse: P. falciparum/malariae vs P. vivax/ovale (hepatic behavior)

P. falciparum & P. malariae
Only ONE cycle of hepatic cell invasion. No dormant liver forms → no true relapse (recurrence is due to inadequate blood-stage clearance/resistance, not hypnozoites).
P. vivax & P. ovale
Form dormant hepatic hypnozoites that release merozoites over months to years → true relapse. Only these two need Primaquine for radical cure.
Fast distinction: If the vignette describes malaria symptoms returning months after apparently successful treatment → think P. vivax/ovale hypnozoite relapse → answer involves Primaquine.

⚖ Do not confuse: Chloroquine vs Primaquine (target stage)

Chloroquine
Blood schizonticide — erythrocytic stage only. NOT active vs liver hypnozoites or gametocytes.
Primaquine
Liver (radical cure) + gametocidal — the ONLY drug for hypnozoites. Poor efficacy for the symptomatic erythrocytic stage.
Fast distinction: They are often combined precisely because they cover different, non-overlapping stages — Chloroquine clears the blood, Primaquine clears the liver + gametocytes.

⚖ Do not confuse: Suramin vs Pentamidine (early-stage African sleeping sickness)

Suramin
DOC for East African sleeping sickness (T. rhodesiense), early hemolymphatic stage. Half-life ~50 days.
Pentamidine
DOC for West African sleeping sickness (T. gambiense), early hemolymphatic stage. Parenteral or inhaled.
Fast distinction: "East" and "Suramin" both start differently but pair by lecture grouping — remember East = Suramin (rhodesiense), West = Pentamidine (gambiense); for advanced CNS-stage disease in either region, think Melarsoprol.

⚖ Do not confuse: Sodium Stibogluconate vs Miltefosine (Leishmania)

Sodium Stibogluconate
Inhibits glycolysis. Parenteral (IV/IM). Added to Paromomycin (17-day course). CI in renal disease/breastfeeding.
Miltefosine
Inhibits fatty acid oxidation. Given orally. Given after a single Amphotericin infusion. CI in pregnancy (teratogenic).
Fast distinction: Route of administration is the fastest differentiator — Stibogluconate is parenteral, Miltefosine is the oral option.

⚖ Do not confuse: Quinine/Quinidine vs Mefloquine (both cardiotoxic, but don't combine)

Quinine/Quinidine
Prolongs QT — cinchonism, cardiotoxicity ("QUeen B-UCCHHH"). First-line IV for severe malaria.
Mefloquine
Also prolongs QT, PLUS neuropsychiatric toxicity ("Mind Floats"). Used for prophylaxis/oral step-down therapy.
Fast distinction: Both drugs independently prolong QT — giving them together is contraindicated due to additive cardiotoxicity, a very testable point.

Exam Traps

Trap: A drug that increases parasite-toxic heme accumulation (chloroquine) does so by blocking detoxification — it does not itself destroy heme directly like Artemisinin's free-radical alkylation does. Don't mix up the two heme-related mechanisms.
Trap: "Radical cure" refers to the liver stage (hypnozoites), not to a drug's chemical radical mechanism — don't confuse this terminology with Artemisinin's free-radical MOA.
Trap: Doxycycline is contraindicated in BOTH pregnancy and young children (permanent dental staining, bone growth effects) and in breastfeeding — Clindamycin is the safer substitute despite an identical antimalarial spectrum.
Trap: A patient who develops flushing, nausea, and vomiting after drinking alcohol during treatment is describing the classic disulfiram-like reaction of Metronidazole, not an allergic drug reaction.
Trap: Halofantrine and Lumefantrine are both phenanthrenes, but only Halofantrine is unsuitable for chemoprophylaxis (cardiotoxicity) and outright contraindicated in pregnancy. Lumefantrine (in Coartem) is comparatively safer and usable in the 2nd/3rd trimester.
Trap: Only Primaquine and Atovaquone act on the electron transport / ubiquinone pathway — a much shorter list than the heme-metabolism group (Chloroquine, Amodiaquine, Piperaquine, Quinine, Quinidine, Mefloquine, Artemisinins, Halofantrine, Lumefantrine, Pyronaridine). Don't lump them together.
Trap: Atovaquone is never used as monotherapy due to a low resistance threshold (single point mutation in Cytochrome BC1) — it is always paired with Proguanil (Malarone).
Trap: Artemisinin monotherapy products have been phased out by WHO mandate — any standalone artemisinin product in an answer choice for "standard treatment" should raise suspicion; the correct answer pairs it with a partner drug (ACT).
Trap: Both Praziquantel doses "paralyze" worms, but the mechanism is increased Ca²⁺ permeability causing contraction then paralysis — this is different from the flaccid/spastic paralysis mechanisms of the nematode drugs (Pyrantel/Piperazine).

Last-Minute Cram Sheet

Malaria — Essentials

  • Only the asexual erythrocytic stage = clinical symptoms
  • Primaquine = only radical (liver) cure + main gametocidal drug. Needs G6PD test. Never in pregnancy.
  • Chloroquine = blood schizonticide only. Resistance via PfCRT. Safe in pregnancy.
  • Artemisinins = gold standard, free-radical MOA, always combined (ACT)
  • Quinine/Quinidine + Artemisinins = first-line for severe/complicated malaria (IV)
  • Never combine Mefloquine + Quinine/Quinidine/Halofantrine/Primaquine (cardiotoxicity)
  • Electron transport pathway = only Primaquine & Atovaquone
  • Doxycycline = 30S; Clindamycin = 50S (apicoplast targets)
  • Antifolates target DHPS & DHFR (Fansidar, Malarone)
  • P. vivax/ovale = hypnozoites/relapse; P. falciparum/malariae = single hepatic cycle, no relapse

Pregnancy Rules

  • Preferred: Chloroquine (Category A)
  • Avoid ("PriMaDonA"): Primaquine, Malarone-caution, Doxycycline, Halofantrine, Lumefantrine, Antifolates
  • IV Artesunate = safe in all trimesters for severe disease

Protozoa & Anthelminthics

  • Luminal amoebicides (Diloxanide, Iodoquinol, Paromomycin) = cyst/carrier stage only
  • Metronidazole = DOC extraluminal amoebiasis, Trichomonas, Giardia. Disulfiram-like rxn with alcohol.
  • Amoebae use PFOR for anaerobic energy — targeted by Metronidazole & Nitazoxanide
  • West Africa early stage → Pentamidine; East Africa early stage → Suramin; Advanced CNS (both) → Melarsoprol
  • Chagas disease → Benznidazole or Nifurtimox
  • P. jiroveci pneumonia → TMP-SMX; Toxoplasmosis → Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine (+ folinic acid)
  • Nematode MOA = paralysis: Pyrantel = spastic, Piperazine = flaccid, Ivermectin = ↑GABA (no adult-worm kill), DEC = immobilizes microfilariae
  • Benzimidazoles bind β-tubulin; highest bioavailability = Albendazole
  • Cestodes/trematodes → Praziquantel (DOC, ↑Ca²⁺ permeability); 2nd line: Niclosamide (tapeworms), Bithionol (flukes)

Classic Exceptions to Remember

  • Atovaquone never alone (resistance via single point mutation)
  • Artemisinins never alone (WHO-mandated combination)
  • Ivermectin ≠ adult-worm killer, only microfilaricidal
  • Doxycycline unsafe in pregnancy AND children; Clindamycin safe in both
